jobs.description: Position overview Salary range: INTERNAL RECRUITMENT TO UC DAVIS ONLY. The Beckley/Herzog Endowed Chair for Enduring Advancement in the Science of Food provides additional funding to a current UC Davis academic appointee in the Associate Professor, Full Professor or CE Specialist title. The additional funding may support the endowed chair holder in areas of teaching, research, or extension activities directly related to the purpose of the endowment. Application Window Open date: September 24, 2026 Next review date: Monday, Oct 26, 2026 at 11:59pm (Pacific Time) Apply by this date to ensure full consideration by the committee. Final date: Thursday, Dec 31, 2026 at 11:59pm (Pacific Time) Applications will continue to be accepted until this date, but those received after the review date will only be considered if the position has not yet been filled. Position description The holder of the Beckley/Herzog Endowed Chair for Enduring Advancement in the Science of Food will be a tenured faculty member or Specialist in the Cooperation Extension (CE) at Associate or Full rank in the Department of Food Science and Technology. The holder of the Chair will be someone who exemplifies excellence in the science of food. Funding will be used to advance excellence in the science of food through innovative teaching, research, outreach, and engagement activities within the Department of Food Science and Technology. The chair is intended to address current and future challenges facing the food system, with particular emphasis on reducing food loss and waste, improving energy and water use efficiency throughout the food system, and advancing biomass utilization. The chair will support scholarship that contributes to a more sustainable, resilient, and efficient food system while strengthening connections among academic, industry, alumni, and public communities. The Chair is for a five-year term appointment and may be renewable based on satisfactory review and at the discretion of the Dean. Responsibilities of the Chair include: • Teach a normal load for the department or provide extension teaching/programs in which the Chair Holder is appointed including student advising and mentoring. • Provide innovation and leadership in research in the area of food systems particularly towards food loss and waste and improving energy and water use within the food systems. • Engage in outreach activities specific to the designated intent by the donor including lectures, conferences, student research. • Perform service to the appointee’s home department and the broader community as expected for faculty at the same academic rank. • Enhance the academic and intellectual life of the campus as a whole. The Chair holder will submit an annual report on the use of the Fund including expenditures of the endowment income to the Dean of the College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences each academic year. Qualifications Basic qualifications (required at time of application) • Associate or Full Rank Professor or Specialist in CE in the Department of Food Science and Technology. Preferred qualifications (other preferred, but not required, qualifications for the position) • Teach a normal load for the department or provide extension teaching/programs in which the Chair Holder is appointed including student advising and mentoring. • Someone who exemplifies excellence in the science of food. • Engage in outreach activities specific to the designated intent by the donor including lectures, conferences, student research. • Perform service to the appointee’s home department and the broader community as expected for faculty at the same academic rank. • Enhance the academic and intellectual life of the campus as a whole. This role requires a strong investigator who will furthermore manage collaborative projects with multidisciplinary research teams and industry partners, mentor trainees at the graduate- and post-graduate levels, as well as track record of competitive extramural grant funding. Additionally, the candidate will oversee regulatory compliance, including IACUC animal protocols, lab inspections, and environmental biosafety standards. Position description Berkeley Law is one of the nation’s great centers for legal education, ever exploring and pushing new intellectual boundaries while tackling urgent, real-world issues. The law school is also known for its vibrant and engaged community of students and scholars who are committed to providing leadership and making a difference on problems of local, national and global import. Currently ranked among the top law schools in the country, the School of Law has ambitious development goals as it looks to continue producing leaders in law, government, and society. Berkeley Law invites applications for a full-time position on our clinical faculty, teaching in our Death Penalty Clinic. This faculty position entails membership in the Academic Senate with rights and responsibilities that are comparable to the standard professorial track, but with an emphasis on teaching, professional competence and activity, research and creative work, and University and public service. Berkeley Law's Clinical Program includes seven in-house clinics: Environmental Law Clinic, Death Penalty Clinic, Global Rights Innovation Lab Clinic, Human Rights Clinic, Policy Advocacy Clinic, Samuelson Law, Technology & Public Policy Clinic, and Social Enterprise Clinic. The Death Penalty Clinic is dedicated to developing students' advanced legal advocacy skills while providing exceptional legal representation to individuals facing capital punishment. In response to the critical shortage of qualified and adequately funded counsel for people on death row, the clinic represents clients primarily in post-conviction proceedings, with a particular focus on jurisdictions that have the fewest legal resources. The clinic also tackles problems endemic to the administration of capital punishment. Through this work, students gain intensive, hands-on experience in complex litigation while contributing to high-quality representation in cases involving the most serious criminal penalties. The mission of Berkeley Law’s Clinical Program is to advance equal justice - racial, economic, and social justice - through three interrelated activities: preparing law students to address pressing societal problems and to become highly skilled, responsible, and reflective legal practitioners; providing first-rate legal services to underrepresented individuals, marginalized communities, and public-minded organizations––locally, nationally, and globally; and producing cutting-edge, interdisciplinary research to support litigation, inform public policy, and increase the effectiveness of our teaching and service. Berkeley Law strives to educate responsible, effective, and forward-thinking advocates who serve the public through legal practice, public policy, academic scholarship, and related fields. Position description The Department of Environmental Science, Policy, and Management (ESPM) at the University of California, Berkeley (UCB) invites applications for a tenure-track Assistant Professor nine-month faculty position in the area of Arthropod Biodiversity. Biodiversity lies at the heart of all ecosystems, from the smallest microbiomes to the global expanses of continents, oceans, and the atmosphere. It holds intrinsic value across many dimensions, encompassing species, genes, functions, processes, and cultures, while also providing tangible benefits such as food, medicine, and other natural products. Biodiversity underpins essential ecosystem services, including clean air, water, and soil, and contributes profoundly to human health, cultural identity, and psychological well-being. Arthropods, which E.O. Wilson famously described as “the little things that run the world,” are the majority of Earth’s macrobiota and have recently faced threats from multiple stressors, including climate change, habitat loss and degradation, and cumulative use of agricultural chemicals. Loss of biodiversity, both locally (α-diversity) and among locations (β-diversity) is occurring at a rate exceeding our current efforts to discover, document, and understand the species with which we share our planet. These patterns are particularly true for arthropods, with insects showing global declines in populations across multiple orders (sometimes referred to as “insect apocalypse”). At the species level, arthropods now represent 70-80% of the documented loss of biodiversity. At the same time, many other arthropods are becoming increasingly problematic as invasive species, pests of agriculture and forests, and vectors of plant and animal pathogens. Expertise is needed in understanding drivers of arthropod biodiversity change, including understanding processes leading to resilient populations, communities, and ecosystems. ESPM is a multidisciplinary community of scholars from across the sciences and humanities who conduct research, teaching, and outreach to advance scientific understanding and develop solutions for the world’s pressing environmental problems. ESPM is home to a top-ranked Ph.D. program in environmental science, environmental studies, and ecological/evolutionary biology. Our undergraduate students have a choice of vibrant majors that span the disciplines in the department. ESPM is committed to addressing the family needs of faculty, including dual career couples and single parents. We are also interested in candidates who have had non-traditional career paths, who have taken time off for family reasons, or who have achieved excellence in careers outside academia. Position description The Department of Architecture at the University of California, Berkeley, invites applications for a full-time tenure-track position at the rank of Assistant Professor in Computation and Design Methods. Berkeley's Department of Architecture sits within the College of Environmental Design, a leader in cross-disciplinary environmental design education since 1959, and is uniquely positioned in the Bay Area, where design practice, technological innovation, and critical inquiry converge in uncommon proximity; for more information, visit UC Berkeley's Department of Architecture. We seek candidates whose work examines and/or demonstrates promise in applying computation as a creative, social, and technical force in architectural design, connecting systems, tools, and intelligent environments to questions of authorship, agency, governance, participation, and the changing responsibilities of design. "Computation and Design Methods" names a broad area of inquiry concerned with how tools, systems, data, media, and methods shape architectural design, representation, research, and practice. Its primary concern is the study and making of socio-technical systems through which design activity is organized, coordinated, and governed, and design artifacts are generated, represented, and evaluated. Possible areas of focus include technically-oriented subjects such as building information modeling, digital twins, spatial data systems, and urban information systems; methodological inquiry such as feedback systems, human-building interaction, participation, distributed agency, and self-regulating processes; and sociotechnical and critical research such as platform studies, civic data, public-interest technology, and built-environment science and technology studies. Across these areas, the field asks how computation operates in architectural design as means, as material, and as media, ultimately shaping how the built environment is experienced and inhabited over time. That is: as a way of making and evaluating design work, as a technical substrate shaped and incorporated into designed artifacts, and as a system that acts back on design practice and culture. This search responds to a moment in which computation is rapidly reshaping design knowledge, pedagogy, and practice. As data-rich, automated, and intelligent systems transform how buildings are conceived, coordinated, evaluated, and inhabited, the need for critical frameworks has never been more pressing. Artificial intelligence, as much a cultural force as a technical one, has generated expectations, anxieties, and professional reorganizations that now bear directly on how architecture is taught, practiced, and understood. The College of Environmental Design’s foundational work on “wicked problems,” feedback, participation, patterns, and design-as-argumentation offers an urgently needed foundation for preparing designers to act responsibly within this transformed landscape, recognizing that technical decisions are inseparable from their human, social, and environmental consequences. Position description The School of Information at the University of California, Berkeley, invites applications for appointment to the faculty at the Assistant Professor rank. Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) is a field of expertise focused on the evolving relationship between people and computing systems. HCI researchers design and study new ways for people to interact, collaborate, create, work, and make decisions with technology, and investigate how emerging computing systems shape human capabilities, practices, organizations, and society. Methods include the design and development of novel systems, experimentation, qualitative and ethnographic research, participatory design, computational methods, field studies, and mixed-methods research. We seek applicants who are defining the next generation of human-computer interaction: developing new ways for people to interact, collaborate, create, work, and make decisions with increasingly intelligent computing systems. We are particularly interested in scholars who both imagine and build new forms of human-computer interaction and rigorously investigate how these technologies shape people, organizations, and society. We welcome research across HCI and related fields, including, but not limited to, human-AI interaction and collaboration, intelligent and adaptive interfaces, social and collaborative computing, the future of work, accessibility, values such as sustainability, privacy, and justice in and through design, ubiquitous and embodied computing, information visualization, human-robot interaction, and emerging interaction modalities. We welcome a broad range of methodological approaches, including the design and development of novel systems, experimental and computational methods, qualitative and ethnographic research, field studies, participatory and critical design methods, and mixed-methods approaches. Successful candidates will demonstrate the potential to establish an internationally recognized research program, contribute to undergraduate and graduate teaching in HCI, and engage with the School of Information’s interdisciplinary community. The School of Information is a graduate research and education community committed to expanding access to information and to improving its usability, reliability, and credibility while preserving security and privacy. Position description The Department of Landscape Architecture and Environmental Planning (LAEP) at UC Berkeley seeks to fill a tenure-track position at the Assistant Professor level. The successful candidate is expected to contribute to contemporary design discourse on “Landscape and Eco-Technology” through disciplinary engagement, teaching, research and/or practice. This position will allow the department to carry forward its legacy of leadership in service of the State of California, the nation, and the wider world. It also will further the department’s disciplinary knowledge on public infrastructure through teaching, design, and/or research in material, vegetal, topographical, and hydrologic landscape systems. We seek a colleague whose approach encompasses cultural meaning and critical discourse as well as performance-based assessment and design engagement. The Department of Landscape Architecture and Environmental Planning at UC Berkeley is California’s flagship program. As an accredited professional program in an R1 institution, the department expects its faculty to carry out research and/or creative practice that is recognized nationally and internationally and to support pedagogy that critically advances the role of Eco-Technology in contemporary design, praxis, and landscape performance. Landscape architecture has a long and distinguished history at Berkeley, starting in 1913 and boasting a renowned cast of alumni and faculty. Today, we offer degree programs at the undergraduate, Masters, and PhD levels. As one of the founding departments in the College of Environmental Design, established in 1959, interdisciplinarity is part of our ethos and public engagement of our mission. Building on the legacy of environmental design, we tackle contemporary challenges from climate adaptation to societal crises across methods, technologies, and media (UC Berkeley’s Department of Landscape Architecture & Environmental Planning). Landscape and Eco-Technology is integral to the resilience, performance, and equity of urban systems. By considering scales and typologies—from site-based construction practices to national climate adaptation strategies, circularity, and carbon policy—we can establish partnerships and enrich disciplinary discourse. Eco-Technology comes into play across topographic, hydrologic, vegetated, and material systems that define contemporary landscape architectural praxis. It requires a synthetic understanding of how landscape systems are connected and are comprehensively designed, modeled, and prototyped. Our department recognizes Eco-Technology as a core competency within landscape architecture, one that is indispensable to the creation of livable, inclusive, and healthy sustainable cities. The successful candidate will help develop courses in the area of Eco-Technology as well as contribute to the department and beyond through collaboration and mentoring. Position description The Berkeley School of Education invites applications for a tenure track position at the assistant professor level in the area of Civics Education, with a focus on civic learning and democratic engagement. We welcome applicants from education as well as a range of connected disciplinary and interdisciplinary spaces, including but not limited to political science, public policy, history, ethnic studies, and data science. The candidate should have research, publication, and teaching and/or mentoring experience in Civics Education with undergraduate and graduate students appropriate to rank. Preference will be given to scholars whose work centers K–12 classrooms and youth civic development. The applicant’s research focus should explore the teaching and learning of civics and advancing learning theory to address the challenges and possibilities of public democratic life. Across the United States and globally, young people express deep concern about polarization, misinformation, civic exclusion, and the fragility of democratic institutions. We seek a scholar whose research program explores Civics Education in ways that respond to these realities and who designs innovations that help educators meet the needs, interests, and aspirations of students. Given the increasing importance of digital citizenship, information literacy, and the civic implications of technology, we would expect the candidate to have some expertise in these areas. About UC Berkeley School of Education In the Berkeley School of Education, we educate like democracy depends on it– because it does. In a fast-changing, polarized world where inequalities and existential threats multiply, education remains an essential lynchpin for fostering human potential, achieving generational progress, and nurturing civic engagement. Together our research, teaching, and practice supports a vision of public education that has as its goal equity and inclusion at all levels - classroom, school, community, district, state, nation, and globe. Our students arrive with exceptional academic talent and professional experience, driven to make a meaningful impact as researchers, educators, leaders, and innovators. Together, faculty and students engage with pressing questions, from how children, youth, and adults learn across varied contexts, to how schools, communities, and societies can expand opportunities and advance educational equity. Through effective and equity-informed education, the BSE helps people and communities learn to dialogue across difference, use critical thinking to make informed decisions, and advance both individual achievement and progress for the benefit of society. As a world leader in public education, guided by a commitment to excellence in scholarship, teaching, innovation, and leadership, our professional and academic programs help prepare the next generation of educators, leaders, scholars, and policymakers, while contributing to transformative knowledge creation and the public good. This position centers on research into how plants or macroalgae and their associated microbial communities jointly respond and adapt to environmental stressors, contributing to climate-resilient crops and microbial systems. The scope of the position spans, but is not limited to: plant-microbiome or macroalgae-microbiome interactions in the context of pathogen defense (viral, bacterial, or fungal disease); soil microbial communities and their role in reducing agricultural dependence on pesticides, fertilizers, and greenhouse gas emissions; and microbial associations with macroalgae relevant to cultivation, health, and climate resilience in the emerging bioeconomy. Research in this position will complement and build on existing strengths in PMB, with opportunities for collaboration through our existing partnerships, e.g. the Innovative Genomics Institute, the Energy & Biosciences Institute, the International Bioeconomy & Macroalgae Center, the Plant Gene Expression Center, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, the Berkeley Food Institute, the Joint Genomics Institute, and the Joint Bioenergy Institute, and other campus and national lab partners. These partnerships support research that integrates fundamental discovery with translational applications for agricultural and environmental resilience. The faculty member appointed to this position will teach and mentor the next generation of scientists in plant and microbial biology, including contributing to PMB's growing undergraduate and graduate curricula in this area. Faculty are expected to contribute teaching to the core curriculum of the department and participate fully in the graduate programs. Position description The Department of Food Science and Technology in the College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences at the University of California, Davis is recruiting an Assistant Professor of Food Microbiology with a preferred emphasis in Genomics and Ecology of Microbial Foodborne Pathogens. This is an academic year (9-month), tenure track Assistant Professor position that includes an appointment in the California Agricultural Experiment Station (AES). Faculty members who hold an Agricultural Experiment Station appointment have a responsibility to conduct research and outreach relevant to the mission of the California Agricultural Experiment Station. Participation in outreach programs and performance of university service are also expected. The appointee is expected to establish a competitively funded research program in the genomics and ecology of foodborne pathogens, including their interactions within complex microbial communities in food systems to address critical or emerging issues in microbial food safety. The successful candidate will develop an internationally recognized research program that advances understanding of how foodborne pathogens persist in various pre- and post-harvest handling, storage, transportation, and processing operations. The program will explore how these pathogens are transferred through food systems by considering genetic, physiological, and ecological properties, with the goal of informing new intervention strategies. Approaches may span molecular genetics, functional genomics, pangenomics, experimental microbiology, and ecological analysis, along with computational biology, data science, and artificial intelligence (AI) /machine learning (ML) methods where applicable to the candidate's research program. Candidates whose work incorporates or extends toward genomic, metagenomic, or ecological dataset analysis, predictive modeling of pathogen emergence and persistence, or the use of AI/ML approaches to interpret large-scale food-system and environmental datasets are especially encouraged to apply, as these are growing priority areas for the department. Emphasis will also be placed on connecting fundamental or applied pathogen research to broader food-system risks. The candidate will be poised to engage across disciplines, collaborating with colleagues as needed to translate biological findings into actionable knowledge for food safety management. The appointee will be responsible for developing and teaching undergraduate and graduate level courses. Examples of existing courses include FST104 - Food Microbiology and FST 108 - Food Sanitation. Furthermore, the appointee will be expected to develop one or more new courses focused on food safety and the genomics of foodborne pathogens. The appointee is also expected to mentor undergraduate and graduate students and participate in curricular development. Participation in and development of public outreach efforts and/or community engagement programs, and performance of departmental and university service is expected. Position description The Department of Plant Pathology in the College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences at the University of California, Davis is recruiting an Assistant Professor of Plant Pathology with an emphasis on plant health and microbiomes. This is an academic year (9-month), tenure-track Assistant Professor position that includes an appointment in the California Agricultural Experiment Station (AES), with responsibility for research and outreach relevant to the AES mission, as well as university service. The appointee is expected to establish a competitive, externally funded research program in plant microbiome science that addresses critical and emerging issues in plant pathology. The program should advance microbiome-informed approaches to the diagnosis, prediction, and/or management of plant diseases and develop science-based solutions to promote plant health. Research should generate fundamental and applied understanding of the composition, function, and/or dynamics of plant-associated microbial communities (including bacteria, fungi, oomycetes, viruses, and/or other microorganisms) and their interactions with plant hosts and each other. Areas of interest may include disease-suppressive microbiomes, dysbiosis and pathobiomes, host-microbiome-pathogen interactions, pathogen-pathogen and pathogen-nonpathogen interactions, disease complexes and multi-infections, microbiome engineering, synthetic communities, and the ecology and evolution of pathogens within the phytomicrobiome. Research may also address climate-driven changes in plant-microbiome interactions and emerging diseases, span model, agricultural, and/or natural plant systems, and should have a strong mechanistic and/or predictive foundation. The appointee will complement existing departmental strengths in plant-microbe interactions, disease epidemiology, and disease management, while expanding microbiome-informed approaches relevant to food security, agricultural sustainability, climate resilience, and the broader One Health framework. The appointee will be expected to teach GDB103: The Microbiome of People, Animals and Plants, a 3-unit, upper-division undergraduate course that serves Global Disease Biology (GDB) and other students. The appointee is also expected to contribute to required GDB courses, such as GDB90: Introduction to Global Disease Biology, GDB 187: Global Disease Biology Seminar, and PMI129Y: One Health: Human, Animal & Environment Interfaces, and will have opportunities to contribute to graduate courses such as PLP201B: Ecology and Epidemiology of Plant Pathogenic Organisms and PLP298: Microbial Ecology. Training and mentoring of graduate students, undergraduate student advising, curricular development, outreach, and departmental and university service are expected. The successful candidate will be an active member of the Plant Pathology Graduate Program and other graduate groups as appropriate and will have opportunities to collaborate with Cooperative Extension specialists and advisors, relevant industries, and other public stakeholders. This recruitment is conducted at the Assistant Professor rank, and the resulting appointment will be at that rank regardless of the appointee's qualifications.

Position description The Department of Psychology at the University of California, Irvine invites applications for a tenure-track faculty position at the Assistant Professor level in health psychology with an anticipated start date of July 1, 2027 (teaching duties will begin Fall 2027). We seek a scholar with strong training in health psychology and closely related areas whose research examines the psychological, social, behavioral, cognitive, and/or biological processes that shape physical health and well-being. We are particularly interested in candidates studying stress, resilience, and health; social and emotional influences on health; psychophysiological or biopsychosocial pathways; health behavior and behavior change; psychological contributors to health disparities; and/or interventions designed to improve health and well-being. Research may address these questions at any point or across multiple periods of the lifespan. The successful candidate will have a theoretically grounded and methodologically rigorous research program that contributes to the core discipline of health psychology. We welcome a range of methodological approaches, including laboratory experiments, longitudinal and intensive repeated-measures designs, psychophysiological and other biological assessments, ambulatory and digital measurement, intervention research, and population-based approaches. We are especially interested in candidates whose work integrates multiple levels of analysis and complements the department’s social ecological approach to understanding health and human behavior. Although candidates may draw upon social, clinical, developmental, affective, or neuroscience perspectives, the position is intended to strengthen the department’s core research and teaching capacity in health psychology. The successful candidate will be expected to teach foundational undergraduate and graduate courses in health psychology, contribute additional courses in their area of expertise, mentor students, and maintain an active program of research with strong potential for external funding. The Department of Psychology values collaborative and interdisciplinary scholarship. Faculty have opportunities to collaborate across the School of Social Ecology and with researchers throughout UC Irvine, including those in public health, medicine, nursing, biological sciences, and related fields and centers (e.g., the Center for Biomarker & Biobehavioral Research). The successful candidate would join the faculty of the Music Department as an Assistant Teaching Professor, and would join the core faculty of UCSC’s Creative Technologies program, a multi-departmental, online undergraduate major whose faculty are dedicated to advanced, innovative web-based arts and design pedagogy, and a curriculum that cultivates imagination, justice, and empowered community in digital contexts. The UCSC Music Department and the Creative Technologies program seek an Assistant Teaching Professor of Sound and Media Arts who will teach courses and mentor students in creative coding, sound studies, and media arts practice including sound art or electronic music. Additional teaching areas may include: generative and algorithmic approaches to design and media; physical computing; interactive, participatory, and/or performance-based digital media; music composition; ethical and critical approaches to emerging technologies in contemporary art; and other courses according to the selected candidate's areas of expertise. The position is situated within a creative community whose practice is grounded in questions of justice, equity, and social engagement–and in which these are not peripheral concerns but central to how we make, teach, and think about art and technology. The successful candidate must have practical proficiencies in one or more technologies from each of the following categories: digital audio workstations (e.g., Reaper, Logic, Live, ProTools), real-time multimedia production (e.g., Max/MSP/Jitter, Pure Data, SuperCollider, Orca), and creative coding environments (e.g., Processing, p5.js, openFrameworks). Note that the category examples are not exhaustive and may include other open-source and/or custom applications. Along with the aforementioned software proficiencies, the successful candidate must have working expertise in one or more programming languages, with preference for those that have relevant application to creative coding, media arts, real-time performance, and sound design/music (e.g., JavaScript, Python, C#). Areas of specialization may include, but are not limited to: Accessibility-focused and disability-justice-focused media practices, including universal and anti-ableist design Critical and historical approaches to sound and listening Spatial audio and immersive media Socially engaged and community-centered practice Ethical and critical approaches to machine learning and artificial intelligence Game art and interactive media platforms The primary responsibilities for Teaching Professors are (1) teaching; (2) professional and/or scholarly achievement and activity, including creative activity, especially as such activities relate to instruction and pedagogy

Position description The Department of City and Regional Planning (DCRP) at the University of California, Berkeley invites applications for a tenure-track Assistant, Associate or Full Professor position in urban planning with a focus on housing. Housing is a core focus in DCRP, reflected in the department's research, curriculum, and public engagement, and in its deep ties to the Terner Center for Housing Innovation, one of the nation's leading applied housing research organizations. We seek a colleague who will deepen Berkeley's leadership in housing research and help shape its future direction. Cities and regions worldwide face intensifying housing challenges, including affordability, climate change, displacement, and homelessness. We welcome interdisciplinary, collaborative, and community-engaged approaches as well. Position description The Department of Neurosciences at the University of California San Diego (UCSD) is committed to academic excellence within its faculty, staff, and student body and seeks a neurologist to lead our interdisciplinary group as Professor and Director of the Parkinson and Other Movement Disorders Center (POMDC). The POMDC at UCSD is committed to the tripartite academic mission of excellence in clinical care, teaching, and research. The center maintains a strong research footprint, supported by a mix of nonprofit, industry, principal investigator-initiated, and NIH grant funding. Participant recruitment primarily comes from patients seen in movement disorders clinics by division faculty. The program is highly translational, with strengths in "bench-to-bedside" treatments and "hospital-to-community" interdisciplinary research. The recruitment of a clinical scientist-physician whose own research program aligns with the goals and resources of the POMDC will enhance the research and clinical aims of the Center. The POMDC and its fellowship program will benefit from a senior clinician-researcher and leader in the field who will play an important role in teaching, patient care, and research and who can, at the same time, step into administrative and leadership roles. The selected candidate will provide outpatient care to movement disorder patients, mentor junior faculty, and teach graduate students, residents, and clinical and research fellows and staff. The selected candidate will work in our hospitals and clinics at the La Jolla and Hillcrest locations and will be encouraged to engage with a wide range of clinical, translational, and basic science programs at UCSD to enhance the national recognition of the Center's research and practice. The selected candidate will also lead the deployment of the program's significant philanthropic endowment and its robust donor stewardship program. Furthermore, the selected candidate will be responsible for maintaining the POMDC's designation as a Parkinson's Disease Center of Excellence by the Parkinson's Foundation, as well as the LBD Center of Excellence designation by the Lewy Body Dementia Association and the Cure PSP Center of Care designation. The appointment will be based on the candidate’s background and experience. Series will include 50% Ladder Rank/50% In-Residence with secured extramural funding or 100% Ladder Rank. Position description The Department of Psychology and the Department of Urban Planning and Public Policy (UPPP) in the School of Social Ecology at the University of California, Irvine, invite applications for a joint tenure-track faculty position at the Associate Professor level in Behavior Change, Decision Science, and Policy. The position will advance research on how individuals and groups make decisions, change behavior, and respond to interventions, institutions, and public policy. We seek scholars who connect behavioral science to important real-world problems with a strong commitment to translating research into effective interventions, actionable programs, and policy solutions. The successful candidate will complement the Department of Psychology’s strengths in basic and applied behavioral research (spanning developmental, health, social, or clinical domains) as well as UPPP’s focus on public policy, inequality, social problems and environmental issues. Interdisciplinary Research and Policy We welcome scholars whose research examines behavior change and decision-making––such as motivation, beliefs, social influence, self-regulation, and risk perception––and connects them to policy design, practice, and broader societal outcomes. We are particularly interested in candidates who bridge individual-level psychological science with social, institutional, community, or environmental contexts. The successful candidate will advance an interdisciplinary agenda that explores both how policy shapes human behavior and how behavioral insights can optimize the design, evaluation, and translation of public interventions and policies. This joint appointment offers rich opportunities for collaboration across Psychology, Urban Planning and Public Policy, the School of Social Ecology, and the broader UC Irvine campus. Teaching and Mentoring The successful candidate will contribute to undergraduate and graduate teaching in Psychology and UPPP. Teaching may include courses addressing behavior change, decision-making, behavioral science, public policy, urban planning, and/or the candidate's substantive area of expertise. The candidate will mentor students across disciplinary boundaries and contribute to preparing students to apply psychological and behavioral science to complex social and policy problems. Qualifications Candidates must have a doctoral degree in psychology, public policy, urban planning, or a closely related discipline by the time of appointment. Candidates should demonstrate: a strong or emerging independent research program; expertise in behavior change, decision science, behavioral science, policy, or a related area; a strong foundation in psychological or behavioral science; potential for interdisciplinary research and external funding commitment to excellence in teaching and mentoring; and commitment to service to UCI and the academic profession. Candidates whose work bridges behavior change, decision-making, and public policy are particularly encouraged to apply. The Department of Theatre and Dance at UC San Diego invites applicants specializing in acting to join a vibrant department committed to shaping the future of the arts by fostering a new generation of creative and collaborative theatre professionals. We are seeking a candidate who can lead a rigorous two year graduate acting progression while also teaching undergraduate courses within the Department of Theatre and Dance. Professorial appointments and advancement at UC San Diego require a sustained record of high-quality and impactful creative work. The position involves active participation in all aspects of the department, including recruitment, casting, curriculum development and a commitment to contributing to the ongoing development of the acting program. The responsibilities of this position include teaching a combination of five graduate and undergraduate courses, ranging from small seminars in the candidate's area(s) of expertise to larger courses that serve both the BA and MFA communities and fulfill the relevant Colleges’ General Education requirements. Position description The Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics in the College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences at the University of California, Davis is recruiting an Associate/Full Professor of Agricultural Economics. This is an academic year (9-month), tenured Associate/Full Professor position with a 20% Instruction and Research (I&R), and 80% Agricultural Experiment Station (AES) appointment. The appointee is expected to establish an outreach and research program in agricultural economics, with a focus on the issues facing California’s farm economy. The appointee will bolster our applied research footprint across the state and help meet the needs of California's agricultural sector through applied research on agricultural production costs and returns, farm-level costs and impacts of regulation, and of management strategies that strengthen profitability and long-run economic viability. The successful candidate is expected to oversee UC Davis ARE's world-renowned Cost and Return studies program (Cost and Return Studies). This will involve supervising research staff, engaging with funders and external stakeholders, as well as maintaining an extramural granting program to support core programmatic activities and methodological improvements. Teaching responsibilities will consist of one to one-and-a-half quarter-long courses per year. The courses to be taught by the appointee will be set by the department chair based upon departmental needs and the successful candidate’s interests/expertise. The appointee’s primary teaching responsibilities are likely to include ARE 120 Agricultural Policy, ARE 138 International Commodity & Resource Markets, 139 Futures & Options Markets, and/or ARE 155 Operations Research & Management Science. Other courses that the appointee may be asked to teach include MS level courses in agricultural economics and finance (ARE 223, ARE 271), and PhD level courses in empirical methods (ARE 202B, ARE 202C), and agricultural economics (ARE 231, ARE 232, and ARE 233). Other responsibilities include student advising at the graduate and undergraduate levels, and training/mentoring graduate students. Performance of departmental and university service at the level commensurate with a tenured faculty member is expected. This recruitment is being conducted at the Associate/Full rank. Position description BTS Biomolecular Engineering Faculty Recruitment Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences Schools of Pharmacy and Medicine University of California, San Francisco The UCSF Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences invites applications for a faculty position. While the goal of the search is focused on junior candidates (to be appointed at the Assistant Professor level), we will consider exceptional candidates with more experience (who could be appointed at Associate or Full Professor). We welcome applications from creative scientists asking fundamental questions and creating innovative technologies to join our interdisciplinary department of investigators. Position description The Department of Film & Digital Media at the University of California, Santa Cruz (UCSC) invites applications for the tenure-track position Assistant Professor of Narrative Film and Media Production. We are seeking applicants whose innovative creative work demonstrates an active and sustained practice in narrative form, expansively defined, with expertise in moving image media, production, and exhibition. Building on the department’s well-established strengths in documentary film and media, social justice-centered approaches to creative practice, and work that critically and creatively engages emerging technologies, we are particularly interested in candidates whose work bridges narrative and documentary practices, engages community-based and collaborative methods, or explores evolving modes and technologies of production. We welcome candidates whose work engages in a broader range of media practices, including interactive, participatory, and immersive media. The position will require the assistant professor to maintain an active creative research practice with a record of exhibition in festival, theatrical, streaming, or broadcast contexts. Our campus follows a schedule of three 11-week quarters per academic year. Our department values interdisciplinary scholarship and practice, and we are interested in candidates who can further expand the skillsets and modalities that we can offer our students. Further responsibilities of the position encompass advising and mentoring undergraduate and graduate students, engaging in faculty governance at both departmental and campus levels, and actively partaking in administrative service for the department, the affiliated college, and the university as a whole. Position description We are seeking outstanding part-time lecturers who can teach or co-teach EDUC 125: Psychedelics Education and the Persistent Taboo on Alternative Ways of Knowing. This introductory course uses psychedelics as a three-part case study to examine: How educational institutions and broader society have adjudicated among competing ways of knowing (i.e., epistemologies, or worldviews). How this process of adjudication has limited psychedelics education and risk reduction efforts that stand to equip students with critical knowledge and scientifically-based tools. How comprehensive knowledge and appropriate campus-based and other tools might support the navigation of complex, real-world contexts safely, rather than assuming pure avoidance of psychedelic substances. Knowledge about and knowledge from psychedelics resides at the intersection of many epistemic traditions and communities of practice, each with their own set of debates, shared agreements, and norms for producing knowledge: neuroscientists, clinical researchers, Indigenous and spiritual collectives, policymakers, and educators. All members of educational institutions - students, families, instructors, curriculum designers, and educational decision-makers - have to decide which communal knowledge traditions they will embrace and which they will reject and, in the ideal cases, reflect on why some traditions count more than others. This course ultimately identifies the unique epistemic, legal, ideological, and practical tensions and alignments that shape teaching and learning about psychedelics. Much like the perennial debates about whether schools should teach abstinence or comprehensive, evidence-based curricula with respect to sex education, alcohol and cannabis education, suicide education, and most recently, digital literacy education, this course is premised on the belief that evidence-based, risk-reduction curricula increase safe decision-making. It is education in the public interest - one of the central tenets of the mission of a public university. In addition to teaching responsibilities, duties include holding office hours, assigning grades, advising students, preparing course materials, and collaborating with program leadership, and other BSE Faculty members. Position description The UCLA Disability Studies Interdepartmental Degree Program is seeking a 50% lecturer for the Spring 2027 quarter to teach an in-person upper division core undergraduate course in the Disability Studies program. Given the interdisciplinary and evolving nature of the field, Disability Studies at UCLA is looking for instructors who represent multiple perspectives, and we encourage applicants from a wide variety of backgrounds to apply. The Disability Studies 101W course asks students to create a critical framework for understanding concepts of disability from a sampling of disciplinary perspectives. This course is organized around the central tension in disability studies -- between disability as lived subjective experience that is both individual and communal, and disability as objective, medical, legal, and sometimes stigmatized category. Students are encouraged to make connections between units and to create their own perspectives on disability in field that defines itself by how it changes. This course satisfies the Writing II requirement as well as the Diversity Requirement for the College of Letters and Science. UCLA has a diverse student population in one of the more diverse cities in the nation; we particularly seek candidates who have taught similarly diverse students in a major research university. Position description The Division of Infectious Diseases in the Department of Medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA is seeking applicants for a full-time postdoctoral scholar position in Computational Immunology and Genomics. The successful candidate will develop and apply computational, statistical, and machine-learning approaches to investigate human immune responses, host genetics, infectious disease, and vaccine immunity. The position will work closely with experimental immunologists, clinicians, and computational researchers and will have opportunities to lead computational projects, develop new analytical approaches, contribute to manuscripts and grant applications, and generate first-author publications. Current projects in the laboratory integrate whole-genome sequencing (WGS), transcriptomics, single-cell RNA sequencing, antibody and systems-serology measurements, PhIP-Seq/epitope profiling, immunophenotyping, and clinical data. A major focus of the position will be identifying genomic and immunologic features associated with variation in immune responses and clinically relevant phenotypes. A Ph.D. or equivalent doctoral degree in Bioinformatics, Computational Biology, Genomics, Biostatistics, Data Science, Computer Science, Biomedical Engineering, or a closely related quantitative field is required. Research activities may include analysis of whole-genome and next-generation sequencing data (including quality control, variant calling, annotation, filtering, genetic association, and biological interpretation), analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data (including quality control, normalization, dimensionality reduction, clustering, cell-type annotation, differential expression, pathway analysis, and comparison of cellular states across clinical or experimental groups), and analysis of high-dimensional immunologic datasets (including systems serology, antibody profiling, PhIP-Seq, flow-cytometry-derived measurements, and related immune assays). Research activities may also include integration of genomic, transcriptomic, antibody, immunophenotyping, and clinical datasets to identify biological signatures and mechanisms associated with immune phenotypes, as well as development and application of machine-learning and statistical models for classification, prediction, feature selection, dimensionality reduction, biomarker discovery, and multimodal data integration. Related research efforts may also include evaluation and implementation of emerging computational and machine-learning methods when scientifically appropriate, development of reproducible computational workflows for processing and analyzing large genomic and immunologic datasets, visualization and communication of complex results to both computational and experimental collaborators, and collaboration with laboratory investigators on experimental design, statistical analysis, interpretation of results, manuscript preparation, and grant applications. The candidate will be encouraged to develop an independent research direction within the broader scientific interests of the laboratory and to contribute to the development of new computational approaches for systems immunology, human genetics, infectious disease, and vaccinology. Position description The Benioff Ocean Science Laboratory seeks a highly motivated postdoctoral scholar to conduct field research on gray whale biology and ecology in the San Francisco Bay. In the last five years, an increasing number of gray whales (Eschrichtius robustus) appear to be using the Bay as a migratory stopover during their 12,000 mile journey between Mexico and the Arctic. Marine mammal biologists have observed gray whales feeding and/or attempting to feed in the Bay, a departure from past migratory behavior that is not yet well understood and that puts whales in closer contact with human activity and often at greater risk of harm, including increased risk of ship strikes. This research is targeted at answering some of the core ecological questions related to understanding how and why gray whales are currently using the Bay and what effects this use of Bay habitats has on the whales themselves. Though specific research questions may be defined in collaboration with the successful candidate, example questions that may be addressed include: ● What San Francisco Bay habitats are most important to gray whales and what are the general temporal and spatial patterns of use? ● What specific benthic prey resources are the whales using in the Bay? ● What is the nutritional value of these prey resources and is there physiological evidence that gray whales are benefiting from access to these food resources? ● To which toxicological risks could gray whales be exposed by feeding upon prey sources within the Bay? ● How may the feeding ecology of gray whales be shaping the ecology of the Bay itself? The specific methodologies will be shaped collaboratively with the successful candidate based on their background and interests and the expertise of project principal investigators. These methods may include: ● benthic ecology surveys and sampling ● direct vessel-based observation of gray whale feeding ecology within the San Francisco Bay ● uncrewed aerial systems surveys ● review and analysis of long-term datasets curated by Bay monitoring and management agencies ● lab-based analyses of whale tissue ● prey energetic analyses ● molecular/eDNA diet analysis ● stable isotope analysis ● contaminant sampling ● acoustic benthic mapping ● ecological modeling The postdoc will work closely with collaborators at UC Santa Barbara, UC Berkeley, the Marine Mammal Center, and additional stakeholders. The postdoc will take the lead in defining field and lab research plans, managing the logistics for accomplishment of this plan, collection and analysis of all data, publishing the results in peer-reviewed journal(s), and communicating about the research with relevant stakeholders. The field research work will be conducted primarily in the Bay Area during the gray whale field season (approximately Jan-May). However, the on-site work location for the remainder of the season will be UC Santa Barbara. Salary is competitive and commensurate with the applicant's qualifications and experience. Position description Professor Henri Drake in the Department of Earth System Science at the University of California, Irvine is seeking a postdoctoral scholar for an NSF-funded project that aims to use computational models to investigate the role of ice sheets in the global Earth System, with a focus on advancing understanding of two-way feedbacks between the cryosphere (grounded ice sheets, floating ice shelves, ice bergs, and sea ice) and the ocean – and their role in global climate dynamics. The start date is very flexible, anytime from Jan 1, 2027 to Sep 1, 2027. The selected candidate will conduct cutting-edge research, including: Developing, running, and analyzing fully-coupled experiments using novel configurations of the Community Earth System Model (CESM3) with dynamic representations of the Greenlandic and Antarctic ice sheets, utilizing two-way synchronous coupling to the Community Ice Sheet Model (CISM3). Evaluating and calibrate newly implemented parameterizations for basal melt and calving Developing and applying new process-based diagnostics to evaluate the fidelity of the simulations, grounded in available remote sensing and in-situ observations. Running mechanism denial experiments to isolate the role of coupled feedbacks. The selected candidate will contribute to our research program and advance their own careers by: Contributing to a supportive, collaborative, and vibrant group culture Collaborating closely with CESM3 and CISM3 developers at NSF NCAR Mentoring both graduate students and undergraduate students on related projects. Disseminating their results through conference presentations and journal publications. Position perks: This is a two-year position that is renewable, pending good progress and available funding. The group benefits from close collaborations with model developers at NSF NCAR (e.g., Bill Lipscomb in this project), DOE’s LANL, and NOAA GFDL, and with field-going observationalists such as Eric Rignot right here at UCI and Andy Thompson at nearby Caltech. The Earth System Science Department at UC Irvine is highly interdisciplinary. It includes 25-30 faculty with broad expertise, all devoted to the study of the Earth as a coupled system. It is a sunny and pleasant place to live, surrounded by beaches, parks, mountains. Position description The Department of Earth System Science at the University of California, Irvine is seeking a postdoctoral scholar to contribute to the ADVIce project (Assessing the Decadal Variability of sea Ice), a US-UK collaboration funded by the NSF and NERC, which examines decadal variability of Arctic and Antarctic sea ice in observations and Earth System Models. The successful candidate will work under the supervision of Dr. Mark England in the Climate Modelling Lab at UCI and collaborate with experts in polar sea ice modelling and variability from the University of Exeter, the British Antarctic Survey and the UK Met Office Hadley Centre. Description of the NERC-NSF ADVIce project: Sea ice at both poles keeps defying expectations: the Arctic's rapid decline has stalled for two decades, while Antarctic sea ice has fallen sharply since 2016. The causes of these decadal shifts remain poorly understood, and unravelling them is essential to anticipating how sea ice will change in the years ahead. ADVIce addresses this gap, studying Arctic and Antarctic sea ice together using models, observations, and reconstructions to diagnose the drivers of these surges and slowdowns in sea ice loss and improve near-term projections. Position description: This is a two-year position, with renewal after the first year subject to satisfactory progress and continued funding. The salary will range from 69,073 to 82,836 USD per year, scaling with experience, see postdoc salary scale, and includes generous benefits, see more information at Postdoctoral Scholar Benefit Plan – UCI. The preferred start date is January 2027, though there is some flexibility for the right candidate. The successful applicant will assess how likely surge and slowdown events are and how their character may change under future warming, drawing on climate-model large ensembles alongside observations and reconstructions. Central to the work, they will design, run, and analyze a new set of CESM2 large-ensemble simulations on the NSF-NCAR Derecho supercomputer that extend existing runs to the present day to capture the recent Arctic slowdown and Antarctic surge periods. The scholar will lead peer-reviewed publications, present at international conferences, and make a research visit to the UK to collaborate with the project partners there. Review of applications will begin on October 1 st , 2026, and continue until the position is filled. Potential applicants are encouraged to apply before this date to receive full consideration. Informal enquiries can be directed to Dr. Mark England at mark.england@uci.edu with the subject ‘ADVIce Postdoc question’. It is a sunny and pleasant place to live, surrounded by beaches, parks, and mountains. Position description Applications are invited for two full-time postdoctoral research positions in Professor Henrik R. Larsson’s theoretical chemistry and computational physics group at the University of California, Merced. Both positions will focus on developing, implementing, and applying tensor-network and related quantum-dynamics methods. Applicants may indicate a preference for one project or ask to be considered for both. The start date is flexible. Position 1: Attosecond electron dynamics This position is part of the DOE-funded Early Career project "Rigorous quantum simulation tools for correlated attosecond electron dynamics in molecules." It will focus on developing and applying tensor-network methods such as TD-DMRG, MCTDH, and TTNS to simulate correlated electron dynamics in molecules on attosecond timescales. Possible research directions include: Ionization dynamics and photoelectron spectra Methods for describing the electronic continuum Multireference electronic structure Vibronic dynamics Selected relevant publications are: Wahyutama, Rano, Larsson, Chem. It will focus on developing and applying tensor-network and related quantum-dynamics methods to simulate vibrational, rovibrational, and vibronic structure and dynamics. Possible research directions include: Quantum dynamics of floppy molecules Molecular polaritonics Potential-energy-surface development Methods for computing molecular spectra Use of molecular symmetry in quantum-dynamics methods Selected relevant publications are: Larsson, Le Dé, Gamboni, J. Position description The University of California Institute on Global Conflict and Cooperation (IGCC), together with the UC Office of the President and UC-managed National Laboratories: the Center for Global Security Research at the Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) and the National Security and International Studies Office at the Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL), are pleased to invite applications for up to six (6) postdoctoral scholar positions in Technology and International Security. Technology has always played a central role in international security. Technology shapes the ways states fight during wartime and compete during peacetime. Today, significant advancements in nuclear technology, autonomous weapons, artificial intelligence, remote sensing, cyber technology, hypersonic vehicles, additive manufacturing, stealth, precision guidance, and other areas have contributed to a widespread sense that the world is again on the precipice of a new technological era. Position description The UCSB Department of Communication is recruiting for a tenure-track/tenured open rank faculty position. Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally transforming how humans communicate, coordinate, and organize across workplaces, institutions, and society. AI increasingly shapes organizational decision-making, collaboration, knowledge production, expertise, and identity while reconfiguring power, authority, accountability, and the boundaries between human and machine agency. These developments create new opportunities to revisit foundational organizational communication theories while also demanding new theoretical and empirical approaches to understanding AI as a sociotechnical actor embedded within organizational and institutional systems. We seek a scholar who conducts innovative, theoretically grounded, and empirically rigorous research using quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-method approaches that addresses the social consequences of AI from an organizational communication perspective. This could include, but is not limited to, topics such as human-AI collaboration; algorithmic decision-making and governance; sustainability; visibility and surveillance; ethics and corporate social responsibility; power and inequality; and (dis)empowerment of underrepresented groups. We are particularly interested in scholarship that advances organizational communication theory by examining how algorithms or algorithmic systems reshape communication processes, organizing practices, and institutional change, rather than only treating AI as a methodological or analytical tool. We anticipate that the faculty hire will make meaningful connections and engage in multidisciplinary endeavors across campus such as the Mellichamp Initiative in Mind & Machine Intelligence, the Department of Technology Management, the Center for Information Technology & Society’s research foci in AI, the Pahl Center for the Study of Critical Social Issues, and campus-wide initiatives in AI and related communities of practice. UCSB is ranked among the top public universities in the United States, and the Department of Communication is also highly ranked in worldwide comparisons. UCSB is a designated Hispanic Serving Institution, and an Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander Serving Institution. It offers several programs to support incoming faculty, including housing assistance (Faculty Housing | Campus Housing) and various grant support programs. Qualifications Basic qualifications (required at time of application) Completed all requirements for a Ph.D. (or equivalent) in a Communication or related field except dissertation by the time of application. Additional qualifications (required at time of start) A Ph.D. (or equivalent) in communication or a related field by the time of appointment, with a desired start date of July 1, 2027 or later. Preferred qualifications Demonstrated research excellence relevant to the job call in the form of research quality, productivity, and a unique scholarly contribution to the area of the social consequences of AI in organizational communication as well as to the communication discipline. Position description The Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of California, Irvine invites applications for two Postdoctoral Scholar positions. Professor Yu Otsuki is seeking two Postdoctoral Scholars to conduct research on the two topics listed below. These positions offer a unique opportunity to develop and evaluate autonomy technologies for real-world construction machinery as large-scale robotic systems, with access to real-world sensor and machine-operation data through close collaboration with industry partners. Topic 1: Autoware-Based Off-Road Autonomous Driving for Construction Vehicles: From Modular to End-to-End Autonomy This topic focuses on developing autonomous driving technologies for large construction vehicles operating in off-road environments. Responsibilities: • Pursue research on off-road autonomous driving for large construction vehicles using real-world field data, with a focus on 1) first establishing a robust modular autonomy architecture for off-road unstructured environments and 2) subsequently advancing toward learning-based end-to-end autonomy. • Conduct research in areas aligned with project priorities, including, but not limited to, perception, planning, localization, sensor calibration, multimodal learning, and other related off-road autonomous driving technologies. Topic 2: Next-Generation Autonomy Technologies for Earthmoving Operations with Heterogeneous Construction Machinery This topic focuses on developing next-generation autonomy technologies for earthmoving operations involving dozers, excavators, and other construction machinery. Responsibilities: • Pursue research directions aligned with project priorities, including, but not limited to, end-to-end autonomy for excavators and dozers, optimization of dozer earthmoving planning, and multi-fleet coordination of heterogeneous construction machinery. Additional responsibilities for both topics include: • Develop, implement, and evaluate algorithms using real-world construction-vehicle data, and integrate research outcomes into the relevant software stack. • Collaborate closely with engineers at industry partners and with researchers at UCI’s Center for Resilient Autonomous Systems. Mentor and guide UCI students involved in the research. • Disseminate research findings through peer-reviewed conference and journal publications and technical presentations. Preferred qualifications: • Experience in one or more of the following areas: autonomous driving, construction machinery, off-road mobile robotics, perception, machine learning, or multi-agent systems. • Proficiency in ROS2, Python, C++, and Git. Anticipated Start Date: As early as mutually agreed upon. This is a full-time, on-site appointment at UCI for an initial term of two years, with the possibility of renewal based on funding availability and performance. Application Deadline: Open until filled. About the Principal Investigator: Dr. Yu Otsuki joined the University of California, Irvine (UCI) as an Assistant Professor in July 2026. He is establishing the Laboratory for Autonomy and Robotics in Construction in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering. Position description Department of Visual Arts at UC San Diego invites applications for an Assistant Professor of Teaching in Film and Media Studies. The Assistant Professor of Teaching will teach in the quickly growing interdisciplinary Cinematic Arts major and will collaborate with The Suraj Israni Center for Cinematic Arts. This center promotes research, scholarship, teaching, production and exhibition of film, providing access and opportunity for UC San Diego students and scholars to pursue instruction in cinematic arts. We seek a candidate who is working across a range of potential research areas, including film and media history, theory, aesthetics, and curation. Teaching will encompass the entire curricular range, from large undergraduate lecture courses to graduate courses for MFA and Ph.D. Art Practice students.
